sections.title: Principles of Management
sections.summary: Quality managers must master core management functions (POSDC), classical and modern theories, situational leadership styles, organizational design across functional silos, HR practices, financial literacy, risk-based thinking, and knowledge management. Three levels of management — top, middle, first-level — each have distinct decision scopes.

concepts.definition: Planning (vision/mission/goals), Organizing (structure & authority), Staffing (right people in right roles), Directing (guide work toward mission), Controlling (monitor & adjust via metrics).
concepts.examTip: Memorize POSDC in order. Each function operates at strategic and operational levels.

concepts.definition: Frederick Taylor's approach: find the 'one best way' to perform a task, separate thinking from doing, standardize processes for efficiency. Foundation of industrial engineering.
concepts.examTip: Taylor = efficiency, time studies, standardization, separation of planning from execution.

concepts.definition: Western Electric studies (1930s) showed productivity rose with both INCREASED and DECREASED lighting. Conclusion: workers respond to attention, not just physical conditions. Foundation of human relations theory.
concepts.examTip: Hawthorne = attention drives productivity. Mary Parker Follett extended this work.

concepts.term: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y
concepts.definition: Theory X: negative — employees dislike work, avoid responsibility, must be coerced. Theory Y: positive — employees want to work, seek responsibility, are creative. Treating workers under X becomes self-fulfilling prophecy.
concepts.examTip: X = coercion mindset; Y = empowerment mindset. Modern quality assumes Theory Y.

concepts.definition: Four-stage cycle: (1) Concrete Experience → (2) Reflective Observation → (3) Abstract Conceptualization (theorize) → (4) Active Experimentation (apply). Cycle continues.
concepts.examTip: Experience → Reflect → Theorize → Apply. Used in adult learning design.

concepts.definition: Antecedent (trigger) → Behavior (observed action) → Consequence (result). Used to identify what causes or inhibits behaviors and design effective reinforcement.
concepts.examTip: A-B-C is a behavior modification framework — exam may give a workplace scenario and ask which letter is missing.

concepts.definition: 9×9 grid plotting Concern for Production (x-axis) vs Concern for People (y-axis). Key positions: (1,1) Impoverished; (9,1) Task; (1,9) Country Club; (5,5) Middle of Road; (9,9) Team Management — the IDEAL.
concepts.examTip: (9,9) Team Management is the ideal. (1,1) is the worst.

concepts.definition: Personal Mastery, Mental Models, Shared Vision, Team Learning, Systems Thinking (the integrating fifth discipline).
concepts.examTip: Systems thinking integrates all five. Senge = 'The Fifth Discipline'.
definitionBullets: **Systems thinking** — see the whole, not just parts
**Shared vision** — aligned purpose across the org

concepts.definition: Autocratic (positional power, no input), Participative (involves people, MBWA), Transactional (clear definitions + resources), Transformational (vision + charisma; Bob Galvin), Management by Fact (data-driven; Baldrige/ISO), Coaching (develop + empower), Contingency (style depends on situation).
concepts.examTip: Match style to scenario. Transformational ≠ transactional.

concepts.definition: Optimizing one part of a system at the expense of the whole. Functional silos foster suboptimization. Concurrent engineering and systems thinking are antidotes.
concepts.examTip: Silos cause suboptimization. ISO 9001, IATF, and Baldrige all emphasize whole-system view.

concepts.definition: All functions (design, manufacturing, quality, sales) work simultaneously on new product/process development. Replaces sequential 'over the wall' approach.
concepts.examTip: Concurrent = parallel; sequential = traditional. Concurrent reduces cycle time and rework.

concepts.definition: Four behavioral dimensions: Dominance (results), Influence (persuasion), Steadiness (cooperation), Conscientiousness (accuracy).
concepts.examTip: Know all four DiSC dimensions and what each emphasizes.

concepts.definition: Four bipolar pairs: E/I (Extraverted-Introverted), S/N (Sensing-iNtuition), T/F (Thinking-Feeling), J/P (Judging-Perceiving). 16 types total.
concepts.examTip: S wants detail; N takes hunches. F considers feelings; T uses logic. E energizes from people; I from solitude.

concepts.definition: Knowledge, Experience, Skills, Aptitude, Attitude. Competency analysis focuses on what's required for the role; differs from job analysis (focused on tasks).
concepts.examTip: KESAA = job competency analysis. Job analysis = task-focused; competency analysis = capability-focused.

concepts.definition: Balance Sheet (assets, liabilities, equity at a point in time), Income Statement / P&L (revenue, expenses, profit over a period), Cash Flow Statement (cash inflows and outflows).
concepts.examTip: All three are required under GAAP/SEC. Memorize the balance sheet equation.

concepts.definition: Cash basis: income recorded when received, expenses when paid (small business). Accrual basis: income when invoiced, expenses when billed (most organizations; more accurate).
concepts.examTip: Accrual = preferred / standard for most organizations.

concepts.definition: Liquidity measure showing ability to cover short-term obligations.
concepts.formula: Current Ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities (target ≥ 2.0)
concepts.examTip: Below 2.0 may signal liquidity risk.

concepts.definition: Net dollar benefit divided by investment. Frequently used to justify projects but does NOT consider time value of money.
concepts.examTip: ROI ignores time value of money. Use NPV/IRR for that.

concepts.definition: Return generated relative to tangible total assets — used when significant capital investment is required.
concepts.formula: ROA = Net Income ÷ Total Tangible Assets
concepts.examTip: ROA is preferred when comparing capital-intensive projects.

concepts.definition: Number of times inventory is sold and replaced over a period. Higher = better cash efficiency, less obsolescence risk.
concepts.examTip: Higher turns = leaner. Industry-specific benchmarks matter.

concepts.definition: ABC allocates costs based on activities consumed by products/services rather than blanket overhead rates. ABM uses ABC data for management decisions. More accurate than traditional cost accounting.
concepts.formula: Traditional: Product Cost = Direct Labor + Direct Material + Overhead
concepts.examTip: Traditional is historical; ABC/ABM is forward-looking and granular.

concepts.definition: U.S. legislation enacted after Enron/WorldCom scandals. Mandates strict financial accounting and personal accountability of top management for disclosure accuracy.
concepts.examTip: SOX = corporate financial accountability. CEOs/CFOs personally certify reports.

concepts.definition: 'Effect of uncertainty on objectives.' Risk can be positive (opportunity) or negative. Managed by identifying, analyzing, evaluating, and treating.
concepts.examTip: ISO defines risk as effect of uncertainty — not just bad outcomes.

concepts.definition: Two lenses: (1) Impact/severity — how bad if it happens? (2) Likelihood/probability — how likely to happen? Replaces preventive action clause from prior ISO version.
concepts.examTip: ISO 9001:2015 introduced risk-based thinking. Two dimensions: impact × likelihood.

concepts.definition: Risk-based approach assessing failure modes, severity, occurrence, and detection. Used for product design, process design, and strategic planning.
concepts.examTip: RPN = S × O × D, each on 1–10 scale.

concepts.definition: Hazard Analysis & Critical Control Points. Risk technique from food industry — identifies process points where preventive action is critical. Applies broadly to QMS.
concepts.examTip: HACCP = food safety origin; rigorous monitoring/record-keeping required.

concepts.definition: Brainstorming-based risk assessment using 'what-if' prompt words. Requires mature/well-defined process and skilled facilitator.
concepts.examTip: SWIFT = guided brainstorming for risk; not for immature processes.

concepts.definition: Graphic risk tool: Causes → Preventive Barriers → Failure Event → Recovery Barriers → Consequences. Visualizes both prevention and mitigation.
concepts.examTip: Bow tie = visual cause-event-consequence with barriers on both sides.

concepts.definition: HRA addresses risk from human error. Poka-yoke (Japanese for 'mistake-proofing') prevents or instantly detects errors. ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.5.1g requires identification of actions to prevent human error.
concepts.examTip: Poka-yoke is required by ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.5.1g.

concepts.definition: Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom. Data is meaningless until interpreted. Knowledge is integrated. Wisdom applies experience and values to act.
concepts.examTip: DIKW pyramid is the foundation of knowledge management.

concepts.definition: Tacit: unrecorded — beliefs, intuition, know-how, skills. Lost when employee leaves. Explicit: codified — procedures, processes, standards. KM aims to convert tacit → explicit.
concepts.examTip: Tacit = in heads; Explicit = in documents. KM goal: convert tacit to explicit.

concepts.definition: Strategically important capabilities that are central to fulfilling the mission or provide marketplace advantage. Cannot be easily copied.
concepts.examTip: Baldrige defines core competencies as strategic capabilities — not just skills.

concepts.definition: Interdisciplinary practice of designing products, systems, and environments for the user, instead of forcing the user to conform. Improves efficiency, safety, and robustness.
concepts.examTip: HFE = design for the human, not vice versa. Reduces errors and increases adoption.

practiceQuestions.q: An organization is heavily siloed and each department optimizes its own metrics, often at the expense of overall performance. This is BEST described as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Suboptimization is exactly this — improving a part at the cost of the whole. Functional silos are the classic cause.

practiceQuestions.q: Which calculation does NOT consider the time value of money?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Payback period simply counts years to recover investment without discounting future cash. NPV, IRR, and DCF all discount future flows.

practiceQuestions.q: A current ratio of 1.2 indicates:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Current ratio benchmark is ≥2.0. A ratio of 1.2 suggests current assets only modestly cover current liabilities — a potential liquidity concern.

practiceQuestions.q: Which Blake-Mouton position is considered ideal?
practiceQuestions.explanation: (9,9) shows high concern for both production and people — the ideal balance.

practiceQuestions.q: Knowledge that lives in employees' heads — intuition, beliefs, and unrecorded know-how — is BEST described as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Tacit knowledge is unrecorded and personal. KM aims to capture it as explicit knowledge before it leaves with the employee.

flashcards.back: Productivity rises with attention, regardless of physical conditions.
X = workers dislike work (coerce). Y = workers want responsibility (empower).
ROI = Net Dollar Benefit ÷ Investment (ignores time value of money).
8.5.1g — requires actions to prevent human error (poka-yoke).

summaryBullets: **POSDC** = Plan, Organize, Staff, Direct, Control (Fayol's 5 management functions)
**McGregor**: Theory X (workers dislike work, need control) vs Theory Y (workers seek responsibility)
**Blake-Mouton Grid** plots concern for production vs concern for people (1.1 → 9.9)
**Senge's 5 Disciplines** for learning organizations: systems thinking, mental models, shared vision, team learning, personal mastery
**3 financial statements**: Income Statement (P&L), Balance Sheet, Cash Flow
**Risk-based thinking** (ISO 9001:2015) replaced standalone preventive action requirement
**FMEA**, **HACCP**, **SWIFT**, **Bow Tie** are the core risk-assessment tools
**DIKW**: Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom hierarchy

sections.title: Communication Skills and Abilities
sections.summary: Communication is sender → filters → message → filters → receiver, distorted by cultural, technical, and psychological filters. Quality managers must master verbal/nonverbal/written modes, three directions (vertical up/down, horizontal), feedback (informative vs corrective), global communication challenges, and information-system-enabled communication.

concepts.definition: Sender → Filters → Message → Filters → Receiver → Action/Opinion/Interpretation/Ignore. Filters distort at both ends — cultural, educational, experiential, technical noise.
concepts.examTip: Memorize the model. Filters exist on BOTH sides.

concepts.definition: Vertical down (top → subordinates: strategy, direction), Vertical up (subordinates → management: status, feedback, complaints), Horizontal/Lateral (across functions: cross-functional teams, sharing).
concepts.examTip: Bottom-up suffers from 'telephone game' distortion. Horizontal needs explicit channels.

concepts.definition: Formal: mandated by SOPs (letters, reports, procedures, performance appraisals). Informal: hallway talk, e-mail, gossip — fast but unreliable, may include rumors.
concepts.examTip: Both exist in every organization. Quality managers need both channels.

concepts.definition: Questions that cannot be answered with yes/no. Plan beforehand, ask open-ended, actively listen and capture responses.
concepts.examTip: Open questions surface root cause and context. Closed questions confirm specifics.

concepts.definition: Paraphrasing, clarifying, asking meaningful questions, and acknowledging the speaker. Speech is ~4× slower than listening capacity — close the gap by engaging actively.
concepts.examTip: Avoid interrupting, changing subject, daydreaming. Paraphrase to confirm understanding.

concepts.definition: Empathy, tact, open-mindedness, sensitivity, trustworthiness, ethics, authenticity, fairness, friendliness. Effective communicators identify with the receiver's needs and interests.
concepts.examTip: Empathy ≠ sympathy. Authenticity = what you see is what you get.

concepts.definition: Informative: passing information, no action expected. Corrective (constructive): intended to cause behavioral change or action — should include positive reinforcement, specific data, agreed-upon timeline, and consequences.
concepts.examTip: Corrective feedback ≠ punishment. Joint planning, not telling.

concepts.definition: Any disturbance that distorts or blocks the intended message — physical (loud environments), technical (e-mail outages), psychological (defensiveness), cultural (language gaps).
concepts.examTip: Asking surfaces dialogue; telling triggers defensiveness.

concepts.definition: Cultural differences (customs, religion), language/dialect gaps, time zones, political instability, organizational structure incompatibility, financial/electronic interface differences.
concepts.examTip: Remedies include glossaries, training, dispatched managers, dispersed-team review, business-hours protocols.

concepts.definition: Operations (record transactions, monitor machines), Day-to-day decisions (cash flow, sales trends, inventory), Strategic analysis (mix decisions, pricing, competitive intelligence).
concepts.examTip: Three tiers — same data, different aggregation and audience.

concepts.definition: Automate tasks, Preview messages, Discipline yourself, Don't duplicate, Stay safe, Block junk + establish e-comm policy, Teach employees filtering tools.
concepts.examTip: Authoritative source: International Risk Management Institute.

concepts.definition: Many organizations spend up to 80% of their big-data budget on cleaning and preparing data — quality of input drives quality of output.
concepts.examTip: Garbage in, garbage out. Data quality is gating for analytics ROI.

keyFigures: Claude Shannon (information theory — sender/receiver model origin)

practiceQuestions.q: In the communication path model, filters can distort:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Filters operate on both sides. Cultural, educational, experiential, and technical filters can distort at transmission AND reception.

practiceQuestions.q: A quality manager wants to surface a root cause from a field service technician. The BEST questioning technique is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Open-ended questions paired with active listening (paraphrasing, clarifying) elicit detailed responses needed for root cause.

practiceQuestions.q: Corrective feedback differs from informative feedback PRIMARILY because corrective feedback:
options: Is intended to cause behavioral change
practiceQuestions.explanation: Corrective (constructive) feedback aims to drive behavioral change; informative feedback simply transfers information.

flashcards.back: Any disturbance that distorts or blocks the message.
Informative = transfer info. Corrective = drive behavioral change.
Up to 80% of big-data budgets goes to data cleansing.

summaryBullets: **Communication path model**: Sender → Encode → Channel → Decode → Receiver → Feedback
**3 directions**: Downward (boss → employee), Upward (employee → boss), Lateral (peer-to-peer)
**Active listening** = paraphrasing, asking clarifying questions, eye contact, no interrupting
**Open-ended questions** start with what/how/why; closed = yes/no
**Noise** = anything that distorts the message (physical, semantic, psychological)
**Informative feedback** = neutral data; **Corrective feedback** = behavior change request

sections.title: Project Management
sections.summary: Projects are temporary, finite endeavors aligned to strategic objectives. Quality managers must navigate the 5-stage life cycle (Initiate, Plan, Execute, Monitor/Control, Close), choose the right methodology (Waterfall, Evolutionary, Agile/Scrum), apply planning tools (WBS, Gantt, CPM, PERT), and use financial methods (NPV, IRR, ROI) to select projects.

concepts.definition: (1) Initiating, (2) Planning, (3) Executing, (4) Monitoring & Controlling, (5) Evaluating & Closing. Stages provide go/no-go decision points.
concepts.examTip: Memorize all 5 stages in order. Each has distinct deliverables.
definitionBullets: **Planning** — scope, schedule, cost, risk, communications, quality
**Closing** — handover, document lessons learned, formal closure

concepts.definition: Sequential phases: Requirements → Design → Implementation → Testing → Installation → Maintenance → Disposal. Best for stable, well-defined requirements.
concepts.examTip: Waterfall = traditional, sequential, requirements upfront.

concepts.definition: Initial capability delivered, then successive deliveries until the final product. Used when requirements are unclear and customer wants flexibility for new tech.
concepts.examTip: Evolutionary = build it in stages, refine as you go.

concepts.definition: Customer collaboration over contract negotiation; Responding to change over following a plan; Working software/deliverables over comprehensive documentation; Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.
concepts.examTip: All 4 are 'X over Y' statements — both sides have value, but Agile prioritizes the left.

concepts.definition: Agile framework for complex problems. Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Development Team. Artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment. Events: Sprint (1–4 weeks), Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Retrospective.
concepts.examTip: Sprint length 1–4 weeks. Scrum Master removes barriers; Product Owner prioritizes backlog.

concepts.definition: Tracks remaining work (y-axis) vs time/days (x-axis). Slope = burndown velocity. Used in sprints to visualize progress and forecast completion.
concepts.examTip: Burndown trends down over a sprint. Flat or rising = problem.

concepts.definition: Hierarchical decomposition of total project work into work packages. Focal point for planning, cost estimating, and assigning responsibility. Each box can show owner, cost, references.
concepts.examTip: WBS is THE foundation for cost, schedule, and responsibility tracking.

concepts.definition: Time-phased bar chart of tasks with start/end dates. Easy to read and modify but does NOT show interdependencies, slack, or uncertainty.
concepts.examTip: Gantt = simple but limited. For dependencies use AND/CPM/PERT.

concepts.definition: Network diagram with single time estimate per task. Critical path = longest path through network = minimum project duration. Tasks on critical path have ZERO slack — any delay extends the project.
concepts.formula: Project Duration = Σ tasks on Critical Path
concepts.examTip: Critical path = longest path (counter-intuitive). Zero slack on critical activities.

concepts.definition: Extends CPM with three time estimates per task: Optimistic (O), Most Likely (M), Pessimistic (P). Used when uncertainty is high.
concepts.examTip: Memorize PERT formula. Weighting favors most-likely estimate.

concepts.definition: Shows task dependencies and timing. Used to communicate sequence and predecessors in larger projects.
concepts.examTip: AND emphasizes dependencies more than Gantt.

concepts.definition: Identifies what tasks need what resources, the quantity per period, and acquisition timing.
concepts.examTip: RRM answers WHAT/WHEN for resources.

concepts.definition: Assigns roles to tasks: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. Resolves ambiguity in cross-functional projects.
concepts.examTip: LRM/RACI answers WHO for project tasks.

concepts.definition: Discounts future cash flows at the organization's required rate of return. NPV > 0 = accept; NPV < 0 = reject. Considers time value of money.
concepts.examTip: Positive NPV = project exceeds required return. Higher NPV = better.

concepts.definition: Discount rate at which NPV = 0. If IRR > organization's required rate, accept the project. Higher IRR = higher potential return.
concepts.examTip: IRR > hurdle rate = accept. IRR can mislead with non-conventional cash flows.

concepts.definition: Number of years to recover initial investment from net cash flows. Simple but ignores time value of money and post-payback returns.
concepts.formula: Payback = Initial Investment ÷ Annual Net Cash Flow
concepts.examTip: Payback is simple but flawed — used alongside NPV/IRR.

concepts.definition: Compares planned value, earned value, and actual cost. Variances reveal cost performance (CV) and schedule performance (SV).
concepts.formula: CV = EV − AC | SV = EV − PV
concepts.examTip: Negative CV = over budget; negative SV = behind schedule.

concepts.definition: Plots probability of risk (low/med/high) vs impact (very low → very high). Each cell drives a mitigation strategy.
concepts.examTip: Probability × Impact = priority. Mitigation depends on the cell.

concepts.definition: Formal document defining purpose, scope, problem statement, goals (SMART), sponsor, funding, team, methodology, milestones, risk criteria, recognition.
concepts.examTip: Charter authorizes and aligns. Required input to planning phase.

concepts.definition: Go/no-go decision points between phases. Outcomes: continue, hold, proceed at funded level, postpone, or cancel.
concepts.examTip: Gates protect organization from runaway projects.

concepts.definition: Compares actual outcomes to predictions in the project plan. One of the MOST commonly omitted steps in the project life cycle.
concepts.examTip: Skipping the post-project audit prevents organizational learning.

practiceQuestions.q: In a CPM network, the critical path is:
options: The shortest path through the network
The longest path through the network
The path with the most tasks
practiceQuestions.explanation: The critical path is the LONGEST path — it determines the minimum project duration. Tasks on it have zero slack.

practiceQuestions.q: PERT differs from CPM PRIMARILY because PERT:
options: Uses bar charts instead of networks
Uses three time estimates per activity
Is used only in software projects
practiceQuestions.explanation: PERT uses optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates: ET = (O + 4M + P)/6. CPM uses a single estimate per task.

practiceQuestions.q: The Agile Manifesto values:
options: Following a plan over responding to change
Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
practiceQuestions.explanation: Agile values customer collaboration over contract negotiation — one of the four core 'X over Y' principles.

practiceQuestions.q: Which financial method considers the time value of money?
practiceQuestions.explanation: NPV discounts future cash flows. Payback period and simple ROI ignore time value of money.

flashcards.back: Waterfall = sequential, requirements upfront. Agile = iterative, embraces change.
The longest path through the network = minimum project duration.

summaryBullets: **5 project lifecycle stages**: Initiating → Planning → Executing → Monitoring/Controlling → Closing
**Waterfall** = sequential, plan-driven; **Agile** = iterative, change-friendly
**Scrum** = Agile framework with sprints (1–4 weeks), backlog, ceremonies
**WBS** decomposes scope into deliverables; **Gantt** shows time; **CPM** finds longest path
**RACI** = Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed (one Accountable per task)
**EVA**: PV (planned), EV (earned), AC (actual). CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV

sections.title: Quality System
sections.summary: A quality system is the documented framework — mission, policy, plans, procedures, audits, reviews — that translates customer requirements into reliable products and services. Effectiveness is evaluated through audits (1st/2nd/3rd party; system/process/product), management reviews, balanced scorecard, customer feedback, and Gemba walks.

concepts.definition: Multiple definitions: fitness for use (Juran), conformance to requirements (Crosby), meeting/exceeding customer expectations, satisfying customer, delighting customer, freedom from deficiencies.
concepts.examTip: Different gurus, different definitions. Know who said what.

concepts.definition: Little q: quality as a department function (QC, inspection). Big Q: quality across the entire organization — every employee, every process, every decision.
concepts.examTip: TQM and modern frameworks demand Big Q thinking.

concepts.term: Quality of Design vs Quality of Conformance
concepts.definition: Quality of Design: building quality in from the start (DFSS). Quality of Conformance: producing to specifications. Both are needed; design quality is the leverage point.
concepts.examTip: Design quality is upstream; conformance is downstream. Improve design first.

concepts.definition: (1) Identify customer; (2) Determine need; (3) Confirm need with customer; (4) Agree on standards/measures; (5) Quantify gap; (6) Define improvement actions; (7) Make improvement; (8) Evaluate; (9) Maintain gains; (10) Repeat.
concepts.examTip: Mission of quality function is collaborative — quality dept doesn't 'produce' quality alone.

concepts.definition: Objectives, process steps, responsibility/authority/resource allocation, standards/practices/procedures/work instructions, testing/inspection/audit programs, change procedures, measurement methods.
concepts.examTip: Quality plan is the bridge from policy to operational practice.

concepts.definition: Macro-level measurement combining financial and non-financial perspectives. Standard four perspectives: Customer, Internal Process, Learning & Growth (Employee), Financial. Some frameworks add Stakeholder.
concepts.examTip: Created by Kaplan & Norton. Drives away from financial-only thinking.

concepts.definition: Leading: predict future performance (training hours, customer satisfaction surveys, employee engagement). Lagging: report past performance (warranty claims, defect rates, financial results).
concepts.examTip: Leading indicators enable proactive management; lagging indicators confirm outcomes.

concepts.definition: Auditor (plans/conducts audit), Client (requested or scheduled the audit), Auditee (organization being audited).
concepts.examTip: Distinguish auditor, client, and auditee — exam may test the relationship.
definitionBullets: **3rd party** — independent registrar audits for certification

concepts.definition: First-party: internal audit by org's own auditors. Second-party: customer auditing supplier. Third-party: independent registrar (e.g., for ISO 9001 certification).
concepts.examTip: 1st = internal, 2nd = customer-supplier, 3rd = independent/registrar.

concepts.definition: System audit: verifies overall QMS appropriateness. Process audit: examines a single process or activity. Product audit: in-depth examination of a specific product against requirements.
concepts.examTip: System (broad) > Process (one activity) > Product (one item).

concepts.definition: (1) Preparation (define purpose/scope, select team, build checklists); (2) Performance (opening meeting, data collection, closing meeting); (3) Reporting/Corrective Action/Follow-up/Closure.
concepts.examTip: Three stages — exam may give a step and ask which stage it belongs to.

concepts.definition: Senior management's informal walk-through of the actual work area, often following an order from receipt to delivery. Reveals reality vs reports.
concepts.examTip: Gemba = 'the real place.' Observations shared with managers but not always formally documented.

concepts.definition: Periodic top-management QMS review (bimonthly/quarterly/annually). Inputs: previous actions, internal/external changes, QMS performance, customer satisfaction, audit results, resource adequacy, risk/opportunity actions.
concepts.examTip: Management review is REQUIRED by ISO 9001 — not optional.

concepts.definition: Senior manager meets with employees 2+ levels below WITHOUT intervening managers present. Surfaces grassroots reality. Must be done with care to avoid undermining direct managers.
concepts.examTip: Skip-level = direct senior-to-floor connection, used judiciously.

concepts.definition: Total cost of achieving quality: Prevention + Appraisal + Internal Failure + External Failure. Prevention is cheapest; external failure is most expensive.
concepts.formula: COQ = Prevention + Appraisal + Internal Failure + External Failure
concepts.examTip: P-A-F-F. Shift spending to Prevention to reduce total COQ.
definitionBullets: **Internal failure** — scrap, rework caught before shipment

concepts.definition: Rate of return where benefits exceed quality costs and failure costs decrease. Quality investments must show financial impact.
concepts.examTip: ROQI = quality version of ROI.

practiceQuestions.q: An ISO 9001 registrar conducts an audit at your facility for certification purposes. This is BEST classified as:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Third-party audits are conducted by an independent body (registrar) for certification. First-party = internal; second-party = customer auditing supplier.

practiceQuestions.q: Which audit examines a single welding operation against process specifications?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A process audit examines a single process/activity. System audits cover the whole QMS; product audits examine specific deliverables.

practiceQuestions.q: In COQ, which category is BEST to invest in to reduce total cost?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Prevention costs are cheapest and reduce all downstream failure costs. External failure is most expensive — prevention prevents it.

flashcards.back: Little q = QC dept focus. Big Q = quality across entire organization.
Prevention + Appraisal + Internal Failure + External Failure.
Customer, Internal Process, Learning & Growth, Financial.

summaryBullets: **Little q vs Big Q**: Little q = product/process quality; Big Q = quality across the entire enterprise
**Quality of Design** = product specs match customer needs; **Quality of Conformance** = production meets specs
**3 audit parties**: 1st (internal/self), 2nd (customer audits supplier), 3rd (independent registrar)
**Audit process** has 3 stages: planning → execution → reporting/follow-up
**Leading indicators** predict; **Lagging indicators** confirm (after-the-fact)
**Cost of Quality (COQ)** = Prevention + Appraisal + Internal Failure + External Failure
**Gemba walk** — leaders go to the work to observe reality, not metrics on a dashboard

sections.title: Quality Models and Theories
sections.summary: ISO 9000 series, Baldrige (MBNQA), TQM, Six Sigma, Lean, and the philosophies of the quality gurus (Shewhart, Deming, Juran, Crosby, Feigenbaum, Ishikawa, Taguchi) form the intellectual foundation of modern quality management. Each model has distinct elements, principles, and use cases.

concepts.definition: Sections 1–3 (Scope/References/Terms), 4 (Context of Organization), 5 (Leadership), 6 (Planning), 7 (Support), 8 (Operations), 9 (Performance Evaluation), 10 (Improvement). Certifiable QMS standard.
concepts.examTip: Sections 4–10 are the auditable clauses. Memorize their topics.

concepts.definition: 9000:2015 — Fundamentals & Vocabulary. 9001:2015 — Requirements (certifiable). 9004:2018 — Guidance for Sustained Success (best-practice).
concepts.examTip: Only 9001 is the certifiable Requirements standard.

concepts.definition: Customer focus, Leadership, Engagement of people, Process approach, Improvement, Evidence-based decision-making, Relationship management.
concepts.examTip: Memorize all seven. Reduced from eight in the 2015 update.

concepts.definition: IATF 16949 (automotive), AS9100D (aerospace/defense), TL 9000 (telecom), ISO 13485 (medical devices), ISO/IEC 27001 (info security), ISO 14001 (environmental), ISO 45001 (occupational health/safety), ISO 22000 (food safety), ISO 50001 (energy).
concepts.examTip: Know which standard belongs to which industry.

concepts.definition: (1) Leadership, (2) Strategy, (3) Customers, (4) Measurement/Analysis/Knowledge Management, (5) Workforce, (6) Operations, (7) Results. Results category weighted highest at 45%.
concepts.examTip: Results = 45% of total. Memorize all 7 categories. Public Law 100-107, signed 1987.

concepts.definition: Visionary leadership, Customer-focused excellence, Organizational learning and agility, Focus on success, Managing for innovation, Management by fact, Societal contributions, Ethics and transparency, Delivering value and results, Systems perspective, plus an integrating value.
concepts.examTip: Baldrige is NONPRESCRIPTIVE — it tells you what, not how.

concepts.definition: Customer focused, Total employee involvement, Process centered, Integrated system, Strategic and systematic approach, Continual improvement, Fact-based decision-making, Communications.
concepts.examTip: Memorize all 8. TQM is a philosophy, not a tool.

concepts.definition: (1) Element approach (tool-by-tool), (2) Guru approach (follow Deming/Juran/etc.), (3) Organization model approach (visit role models), (4) Japanese approach (Deming Prize methods), (5) Award criteria approach (use Baldrige/Deming criteria).
concepts.examTip: 5 ways to implement TQM — exam may give a scenario and ask which approach.

concepts.definition: Kaizen: nonstop incremental, orderly continuous improvement (Japanese). Kaizen Blitz/Event: 5-day intensive structured event focused on eliminating waste and reducing costs.
concepts.examTip: Kaizen = ongoing philosophy. Kaizen blitz = focused 5-day project.

concepts.definition: (1) Internal: across functions or locations within own org; (2) Competitive: direct competitors; (3) Functional: same function in non-competitor; (4) Generic: any process in any industry.
concepts.examTip: Internal → Competitive → Functional → Generic in increasing scope/difficulty.

concepts.definition: Determine what to benchmark → Define existing process → Form team → Identify partners → Collect/analyze data → Evaluate vs partner → Determine impact → Set new targets → Implement & monitor → Repeat.
concepts.examTip: Benchmarking is iterative, not one-shot.

concepts.definition: Father of Statistical Quality Control. Created the control chart and the PDCA cycle (often misattributed to Deming). Distinguished assignable causes from chance (common) causes of variation. Bell Labs, 1931.
concepts.examTip: Shewhart = SPC + PDCA + control chart + variation theory.

concepts.definition: Authored the 14 Points for Transformation, the 7 Deadly Diseases, and the System of Profound Knowledge (Appreciation for system, Theory of knowledge, Knowledge about variation, Psychology). Promoted PDSA over PDCA.
concepts.examTip: 14 Points + 7 Diseases + 4 components of profound knowledge. Drove out fear (Point 8).

concepts.definition: Constancy of purpose; new philosophy; cease dependence on inspection; end price-only awards; improve constantly; institute training; institute leadership; drive out fear; break down barriers; eliminate slogans; eliminate quotas; remove pride-of-workmanship barriers; education/self-improvement program; everyone works on transformation.
concepts.examTip: Know the 14 Points by theme. 'Drive out fear' (#8) and 'cease dependence on inspection' (#3) are commonly tested.

concepts.definition: (1) Lack of constancy of purpose; (2) Short-term profit emphasis; (3) Performance reviews/merit ratings; (4) Mobility of management; (5) Running on visible figures alone; (6) Excessive medical costs; (7) Excessive warranty costs.
concepts.examTip: #3 (annual performance reviews) and #5 (visible figures only) are uniquely controversial.

concepts.definition: (1) Quality Planning; (2) Quality Control (measure → compare to goal → act on gap); (3) Quality Improvement (prove need → infrastructure → project teams → diagnose → control to hold gains).
concepts.examTip: Juran's trilogy: Plan, Control, Improve. Pareto principle credited to Juran.
definitionBullets: **Quality Planning** — identify customers, determine needs, design product/process
**Quality Control** — measure performance, compare to goals, act on differences
**Quality Improvement** — prove need, identify projects, diagnose causes, remedy

concepts.definition: Two journeys for improvement: Diagnostic (symptom → cause) and Remedial (cause → remedy). Foundation of structured problem-solving.
concepts.examTip: Diagnostic journey first, then remedial.

concepts.definition: (1) Quality = conformance to requirements; (2) No quality problem — always cheaper to do right first time; (3) Only performance measurement is cost of quality; (4) Only performance standard is zero defects; (5) Quality from prevention, not detection.
concepts.examTip: Crosby = zero defects + COQ + prevention. Conformance to requirements is his definition of quality.
definitionBullets: Measurement = price of nonconformance (cost of quality)
There is no such thing as a 'quality problem' — quality is free

concepts.definition: Quality as a strategic business tool requiring awareness across the entire organization. Three responsibility areas: Quality Leadership, Quality Technology, Organizational Commitment. Coined 'Total Quality Control' — predecessor to TQM.
concepts.examTip: Feigenbaum = TQC; quality is strategic, not just shop floor.

concepts.definition: Created the cause-and-effect (fishbone/Ishikawa) diagram. Promoted quality circles. Defined 4 audit types: by president, by unit head, by QC staff, mutual QC audit. Emphasized 'respect for humanity' and full participation.
concepts.examTip: Ishikawa = fishbone + quality circles + 4 audit types.

concepts.definition: Quality is the loss imparted to society from the time the product is shipped. Any deviation from target = loss. Drives continuous improvement beyond mere spec compliance.
concepts.examTip: Taguchi loss is QUADRATIC in distance from target. Closer to target = better.

concepts.definition: Design of Experiments (DOE) for parameter design, tolerance design, and robust design. Identifies design settings that minimize variation in the presence of noise factors.
concepts.examTip: Taguchi DOE = robust design. Different from classical DOE.

keyFigures: Walter A. Shewhart (SPC, control charts, PDCA)
W. Edwards Deming (14 Points, Profound Knowledge)
Ronald Reagan (signed Public Law 100-107 establishing MBNQA, 1987)

practiceQuestions.q: The Baldrige Award category weighted highest is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Results is weighted at 45% — higher than any of the other six categories.

practiceQuestions.q: Crosby's definition of quality is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Crosby defined quality as conformance to requirements. Juran defined it as fitness for use.

practiceQuestions.q: The PDCA cycle was originally developed by:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Shewhart developed PDCA at Bell Labs. Deming popularized it (he advocated PDSA — Plan-Do-Study-Act).

practiceQuestions.q: Taguchi's loss function states that loss to society is:
options: Zero as long as the product is within specification limits
practiceQuestions.explanation: L(y) = k(y − m)² — quadratic. The further from target, the loss grows by the square of deviation, regardless of being within spec.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of Deming's 14 Points is MOST closely associated with employee psychological safety?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Point 8 — 'Drive out fear' — directly addresses psychological safety as essential for transformation.

flashcards.back: 10 sections (1-3 intro; 4-10 auditable: Context, Leadership, Planning, Support, Operations, Performance Evaluation, Improvement).
Leadership, Strategy, Customers, Measurement/Analysis/KM, Workforce, Operations, Results.
Quality Planning, Quality Control, Quality Improvement.
Conformance to requirements; do it right first time; cost of quality; zero defects; prevention.
L(y) = k(y − m)² — quadratic with deviation from target m.
Customer focus, total involvement, process centered, integrated system, strategic approach, continual improvement, fact-based, communications.

summaryBullets: **ISO 9001:2015** has 10 sections; built on 7 quality management principles
**ISO 9000** = vocabulary; **9001** = requirements; **9004** = guidance for sustained success
**Baldrige (MBNQA)** — 7 categories: Leadership, Strategy, Customers, Measurement, Workforce, Operations, Results
**TQM** has 8 primary elements; built on customer focus + continuous improvement + employee involvement
**Deming**: 14 Points + 7 Deadly Diseases + PDCA
**Juran's Trilogy**: Quality Planning, Quality Control, Quality Improvement
**Crosby's 5 Absolutes**: Quality = conformance to requirements; prevention, not appraisal; zero defects standard; cost of quality; quality is free
**Ishikawa**: father of QC circles, fishbone diagram, 7 basic QC tools
**Taguchi**: loss function — any deviation from target = loss to society
